keywords: why invest in deepgrid
title: The investment case
lead: DeepGrid Semi is a fabless semiconductor company building a single 28 nm, six-chiplet automotive SoC that underpins fifteen products across ADAS, defence, and industrial autonomy, all from one tapeout. India's ADAS mandates on commercial vehicles create a legislated demand pool of roughly one million units a year, and no indigenous silicon exists at this stage to serve it at a price the market can pay.
explanation: The Demand Floor: India has written specific ADAS functions, drowsiness detection, blind-spot monitoring, lane-departure warning, into law for commercial vehicles, with new models from April 2026 and the existing fleet from October. Roughly one million N2/N3 trucks a year fall in scope, making the buying decision a matter of when, not whether. This legislative trigger converts what would otherwise be a discretionary technology sale into a compliance obligation, giving DeepGrid a demand floor that is not dependent on OEM discretion alone. Management projects the plan captures 1.8% of that pool by FY2032.

The Cost Wedge: Foreign silicon prices India out, an imported ADAS module costs multiples of the kit price this market can pay, and no indigenous alternative exists at this stage. Western incumbents' compute board BOMs exceed $6,000, forcing them to target premium, high-margin logistics networks in developed markets. DeepGrid's kit is described as 3–7× cheaper than any import because it owns the chip inside it, and software-only autonomy platforms are structurally squeezed by having to purchase expensive merchant silicon compute engines, a margin trap DeepGrid avoids through vertical integration.

The Platform Multiplier and the Real Risk: One tapeout, structured as $3.17 M across four gated stages, with six of nine de-risking milestones already marked done, seeds four business lines, with management projecting ₹1,128 Cr in FY2032 revenue per the Investment Memorandum; the investor brief separately states ₹1,388 Cr by FY32, and both are management projections contingent on this raise. The central risk the memorandum itself names is schedule: qualified silicon lands H1 2028, after every mandate date, and OEM design-in runs 18–30 months, meaning the next two years are an FPGA business sold through government and PSU channels. Two products carry 64% of projected revenue, so a single certification delay hits ₹720 Cr of the plan simultaneously.

Concentration Risk: Two products carry 64% of the ₹1,128 Cr revenue plan, a single certification delay hits ₹720 Cr at once.
Proof of Execution: A 130 nm tapeout is already done, the perception stack runs at 40 fps on FPGA today, and ₹1.01 Cr is contracted via MCEME, pre-revenue but not pre-product.

keywords: why is the demand real
title: The demand is legislated, not forecast
lead: The demand is anchored in gazette-notified law, not market forecasts: MoRTH has mandated AEBS on all N2/N3 commercial vehicles by October 2027 and four further ADAS functions, drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off, and lane-departure warning, on new models by October 2027 and all models by January 2028. Management sizes the reachable pool at approximately 1.0 million units annually, comprising ~500k new N2/N3 units and a ~500k retrofit pool, and describes this as a regulatory floor, not a forecast.
explanation: The Legislative Clock: India's Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has notified phased, function-specific compliance deadlines in the Gazette, replacing discretionary adoption with legal obligation. AEBS (AIS-162, CMVR 96(12)) binds new models from 1 January 2027 and all models from 1 October 2027; drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off, and lane-departure warning (AIS-184/186/187/188, CMVR 125Q and 98(6)) bind new models from 1 October 2027 and all models from 1 January 2028. These dates are gazette-notified and have been independently reported as effective, aligning India's commercial vehicle safety regime with European standards. Because compliance is a condition of continued operation rather than a purchasing preference, the demand does not depend on buyer sentiment.

The Bundling Argument: Four functions arriving on one compliance clock creates a structural procurement advantage for any supplier that covers more than one function from a single perception core. Management states that a supplier carrying multiple functions from one core is materially easier to nominate than four separate suppliers, and that this bundling logic, rather than any single function, is the primary design-in argument. Two additional mandates stack on top: AIS-140 requires GPS and driver-behaviour monitoring on commercial fleets, and the S100 chiplet carries that telematics interface natively in every kit at no added cost; AIS-004 puts LDWS, FCWS, and LKAS on all new M-category vehicles, creating aftermarket retrofit pull for the ₹50,000 mirror product. Post-2022 semiconductor supply fragility has further prompted Indian OEMs to seek domestic chip partners, reinforcing the commercial case.

Where the Sources Diverge: The Investment Memorandum and the Information Memorandum both describe the AD2 truck kit as mandate-driven and characterise demand as a regulatory floor. However, an internal research finding flags a direct contradiction on the AD0 Smart Mirror: the Revenue Build sheet labels it 'AD0 Smart Mirror (mandate retrofit)' while the Demand & TAM sheet states it is 'NOT mandated, voluntary safety/convenience buy.' The AD0 line represents 54,000 units and management-projected FY2032 revenue of ₹270 Cr, equal to 23.9% of the plan; which characterisation is correct materially affects the risk profile and sales-cycle assumptions for nearly a quarter of projected group revenue. Investors should treat the AD0 demand basis as unresolved until the two internal documents are reconciled.
facts: Mandate Pool: ~1.0M units annually, ~500k new N2/N3 vehicles plus ~500k retrofit, described by management as a regulatory floor, not a forecast.
Compliance Deadlines: AEBS mandatory on all N2/N3 models by 1 October 2027; drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off, and lane-departure warning mandatory on all models by 1 January 2028.

Market Context: India ADAS aftermarket TAM cited at ₹61,000 Cr by 2030, against current ADAS penetration below 5% across 70 million vehicles, the lowest among all major auto markets (management projection).

AD0 Demand Dispute: Internal documents disagree, Revenue Build calls the ₹270 Cr, 54,000-unit AD0 mirror 'mandate retrofit'; Demand & TAM sheet calls it 'NOT mandated, voluntary buy', leaving 23.9% of FY2032 projected revenue on an unresolved basis.

keywords: how big is the market
title: Market size
lead: The India ADAS aftermarket TAM stands at ₹61,000 Cr by 2030, with a mandate-specific SAM of ₹85,000 Cr (5M+ N2/N3 trucks under GSR 184(E)) and a DGrid-addressable mandate-wave opportunity of ₹8,500 Cr. The global ADAS market reaches $83.98B by 2027, while India's broader retrofit market across 9 crore vehicles is sized at ₹4,50,000 Cr.
explanation: The Regulatory Floor: The primary demand driver is MoRTH GSR 184(E), which makes ADAS mandatory on all N2/N3 commercial trucks from April 2026, creating a captive retrofit and OEM market of 5M+ trucks. This is described as a regulatory floor, not a forecast, meaning the demand is legislated rather than dependent on voluntary adoption. The ADAS penetration across India's 70M vehicles currently sits below 5%, the lowest among all major auto markets, which defines the scale of the gap the mandate is designed to close. A separate AIS-004 mandate covers LDWS, FCWS and LKAS on all new M-category vehicles from 2025, adding a further pull for the AD0 kit at ₹50,000.

The Sizing Layers: Multiple market figures appear across documents and serve different purposes. The India ADAS aftermarket TAM is ₹61,000 Cr by 2030 (IM, June and Aug 2026); the India SAM for mandated N2/N3 trucks is ₹85,000 Cr; the retrofit market across 9 crore vehicles is ₹4,50,000 Cr; and the DGrid-addressable mandate-wave opportunity is ₹8,500 Cr, all from the same pricing slide in both IM versions. The Business Plan market sheet separately sizes the mandated ADAS annual TAM at $200M (Telematicswire/Roadzen on GSR 184(E)) and the SAM at 1M units of N2/N3 trucks (approximately 500k new per year plus 500k retrofit). The global ADAS market figure of $83.98B by 2027 is a global reference point, not the serviceable market; documents explicitly note that near-term addressable market is the India slice, where DeepGrid's share is materially higher than the single-digit global capture percentages shown.

The Structural Constraint: Market size and addressable market diverge sharply because of Indian trucking's ownership structure. Of 12.5M trucks on Indian roads operated by 3.5M operators, 75–80% of operators own fewer than five trucks and move 85% of India's freight, a segment that cannot be sold into directly at any realistic cost of acquisition. This means the 5M+ mandated base is not fully reachable through a direct sales force, and the plan's addressable segment is narrowed to organised fleets of 50+ trucks and OEM/Tier-1 line-fit relationships. Management projects FY32 AD2 volume at 18,000 units, which is 0.36% (1.8% unit share) of the 1M mandated truck pool, a figure the business plan describes as more credible, not less, precisely because of this structural reality.
facts: India ADAS Aftermarket TAM: ₹61,000 Cr by 2030, covering 3M+ addressable fleet vehicles under the GSR 184(E) mandate.
India SAM (Mandated Trucks): ₹85,000 Cr representing 5M+ N2/N3 trucks; DGrid-addressable mandate-wave subset is ₹8,500 Cr.
Global ADAS Market: $83.98B by 2027 (management reference figure); India ADAS market $2.29B in 2024 growing at 20.6% CAGR to ~$14.9B by 2034 (EMR).
Management Projection, FY32 Unit Capture: 18,000 AD2 kits, equal to 0.36% of the 1M mandated N2/N3 truck pool, described as a demand floor not a forecast.

keywords: who buys, and how does deepgrid reach them
title: Customers and go-to-market
lead: DeepGrid reaches buyers through six distinct procurement routes off a single bill of materials, spanning regulated Tier-1 ADAS suppliers, CV OEMs, government and PSU fleets via GeM, state transport undertakings, and autonomous fleet operators. The sequencing is deliberate: the GeM/PSU route is transactable today on eligibility alone, while the larger mandate-driven Tier-1 and OEM channels open from 2027 onward as certification milestones are cleared.
explanation: The Regulated Mandate Channel: The primary commercial path runs through braking Tier-1 suppliers and CV OEMs who must source AEBS, blind-spot, drowsiness, and lane-departure functions under CMVR rules binding from 1 January 2027 for new models and 1 October 2027 for all models. DeepGrid positions itself as a Tier-2 perception supplier, delivering object lists, TTC estimates, and sensor-health states, while the Tier-1 retains brake actuation, homologation, and warranty. The decision-room for UC-01 includes the braking Tier-1's functional-safety manager, the CV OEM's chief engineer, and ARAI or ICAT as the approving body. Because four of the five mandated functions bind on one shared perception core, a supplier carrying several from one SoC is easier for an OEM to nominate than four separate vendors.

The Government and PSU Wedge: The only route that can generate revenue before qualified silicon exists is the GeM listing for state transport undertakings, PSU fleets, and municipal operators under the PPP-MII Order 2017 (revised 2020) and GFR 153(iii). At or above 50% local content, DeepGrid earns a 20% margin of purchase preference and a right to match, and the gate is eligibility rather than safety certification. Every unit delivered under this route is instrumented, with telemetry rights secured in the supply contract, making these vehicles the evidence engine for the nuisance-suppression benchmark needed for UC-02. The risk is that an incumbent already draws approximately 30% of its revenue from these tenders and can underbid on empanelment.

The Indirect and Fleet Channels: Beyond the mandate and government routes, the GTM strategy calls for Tier-1 channel alliances, with named candidates such as Uno Minda, Spark Minda, or Bosch India, where DeepGrid acts as a Tier-2 technology licensor of its ASIC and perception software, and the Tier-1 handles ECU assembly, integration, and OEM relationships with Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, and Mahindra. This indirect model is planned for months 18–36 as the ASIC transitions from MPW prototyping to high-volume production. Separately, the fleet and mobility segment, management-projected at ₹88.7 Cr and 7.9% of FY2032 revenue, addresses autonomous TaaS operators at ₹66 L per vehicle and port autonomy customers such as Vizag Container Terminal, where a live order is already cited.
facts: GeM Route Timing: UC-06 (Government/PSU kit) is transactable now, the only use case that does not wait for 2027 mandate dates, with the gate being a live GeM listing at ≥50% local content and one Class-I tender bid submitted.

Smart Truck Concentration: The AD2 Smart Truck kit is management-projected at ₹450 Cr in FY2032, representing 39.9% of the plan at 18,000 units and ₹2,50,000 per unit, making it the single largest SKU and the primary mandate-channel product.

Tier-1 Partnership Model: Under the indirect channel, DeepGrid licenses its ASIC and perception software to domestic Tier-1 suppliers who handle ECU assembly, validation, and OEM line-fit design-wins with truck makers including Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, and Mahindra.

Fleet and Mobility Revenue: The fleet and mobility segment comprises two SKUs, Autonomous TaaS (₹66 Cr, 5.8% of FY2032 plan, first revenue FY2028) and Seaport AGV, with the highest revenue per unit in the portfolio at ₹66 L per TaaS vehicle; these are management projections.

keywords: how do the fifteen products fit together
title: One chip, fifteen products
lead: All fifteen products run a single SoC2 die, one 57 mm² 28 nm tapeout, not fifteen independent silicon bets, organised across four parts: Road Autonomy (3 SKUs, ₹762 Cr, 67.5% of FY2032 revenue), Silicon & Compute (5 SKUs, ₹194 Cr, 17.2%), Fleet & Mobility (2 SKUs, ₹88.7 Cr, 7.9%), and Sensors & Robotics (5 SKUs, ₹83.5 Cr, 7.4%). The portfolio logic is that 74% of the SoC2 frame is unused by any single product, so the same mask and firmware stack supports the full range without a second tapeout.
explanation: The Shared Foundation: Every SKU in the portfolio runs the same SoC2 silicon under different firmware, one tapeout, not fifteen independent product bets. The die integrates six chiplets (A100 Vehicle AI, R100 Radar, T100 Edge AI, D100 Defence compute, S100 Vehicle gateway, H100 Health AI) on a single ~57 mm² part that fuses eleven sensor channels in 8.6 ms of a 33.3 ms frame. Because 74% of that frame remains unused by any one product, the headroom is what makes the portfolio possible: each additional SKU draws on spare silicon capacity rather than requiring new masks. The cost advantage is structural, building the six chiplets as separate dies would cost approximately $18M in tapeouts; as one combo die the engineering estimate is approximately $5M.

The Revenue Architecture: The portfolio layers hardware sales with recurring revenue streams sitting on top of every product rung, SaaS at ₹5K–₹25K per vehicle per year, Autonomous Truck DaaS at ₹2.5L/truck/yr (93% gross margin), seaport AGV fleet operations at ₹45.3L/AGV/yr (92% gross margin), and fleet-health SaaS through the H100 wearable at ₹8L/truck/yr, with recurring revenue projected to reach ₹116 Cr by FY2032. Six distinct buyer routes, government, PSU, Tier-1 OEM, fleet operator, defence, and industrial, are intended to prevent procurement concentration from matching revenue concentration. The investment memorandum notes, however, that the fifteen revenue lines reach market through genuinely different procurement motions, which is what keeps concentration risk from being total rather than eliminating it.
facts: Portfolio Split: Four parts, Road Autonomy ₹762 Cr (67.5%), Silicon & Compute ₹194 Cr (17.2%), Fleet & Mobility ₹88.7 Cr (7.9%), Sensors & Robotics ₹83.5 Cr (7.4%), all management projections for FY2032.
Concentration Risk: Smart Truck (₹450 Cr, 39.9%) and Smart Mirror (₹270 Cr, 23.9%) together represent approximately 64% of projected FY2032 group revenue from two SKUs in one product family.

Silicon Efficiency: One ~57 mm² 28 nm die with six chiplets fuses eleven sensor channels in 8.6 ms of a 33.3 ms frame, leaving 74% of the frame unused, the headroom that makes fifteen products viable on one mask.

Tapeout Economics: Six chiplets built as separate dies carry an engineering estimate of ~$18M in tapeout costs; combined as one combo die the estimate is ~$5M, the saving that funds the portfolio breadth.

lead: DeepGrid's 28 nm silicon is a single ~57 mm² die carrying six chiplets, A100, R100, T100, D100, S100 and H100, fabricated at TSMC and designed in-house at an estimated ~$3 M tapeout cost. Each chiplet is treated as a separate business unit, A100 for vehicle AI, R100 for radar, T100 for edge AI, D100 for defence compute, S100 for vehicle gateway telematics, and H100 for driver-health AI, meaning a competitor seeking to replicate the full capability would require six separate tapeouts. The design cost is cited as approximately $3 M, contrasted with Nvidia's $100 M+ spend on comparable efforts.

Verification Status and Figures: PrimeSoC returned a FEASIBLE verdict on the architecture in March 2026, and SoC2 tapeout is planned for Q4 2026, funded by the current raise. The die cost is stated as approximately $30 in the Information Memorandum, enabling a ₹2 L system kit versus an ₹8 L import-dependent alternative, a 3–7× cost advantage attributed directly to owning the silicon. Memory bandwidth is cited as 102.4 GB/s of LPDDR5; all frame-rate and throughput figures in the materials are management projections, not third-party benchmarks.

Radar Differentiation: R100 chiplet uses a 12-bit native radar ADC; all cited competitors re-quantise to INT16, reducing dynamic range in adverse weather.
Tapeout Economics: Design cost ~$3 M; die cost ~$30 per unit, enabling a ₹2 L kit price versus ₹8 L for import-dependent alternatives (3–7× below every import, per management).

lead: DeepGrid's core defensibility rests on vertical integration across silicon, AI models, and systems, a combination no other Indian startup currently replicates. The company claims to be the only Indian startup designing a vertically integrated, single-die ADAS combo-die for commercial vehicles, with India-specific perception models and 39.3 TOPS deep-learning acceleration that domestic software-first and microcontroller peers structurally lack.
explanation: The Silicon Moat: DeepGrid owns the full stack, chip, AI models, and system, which is the structural argument against both software-only and chip-only competitors. Pure-play ADAS software players are being squeezed from above by OEMs absorbing the stack and from below by chipmakers pushing up; DeepGrid's position across all three layers means the compression that threatens point players is the consolidation it is built to win. Domestic software-first peers such as Minus Zero and Swaayatt are structurally squeezed by expensive imported merchant silicon, while microcontroller/SoC peers such as Mindgrove and Netrasemi lack the 39.3 TOPS deep-learning acceleration and specialised 77 GHz radar processing required for real-time safety.

Management projects the T100 AI Licence, which packages these Indian road perception models as a recurring SDK subscription, reaches first revenue in FY2029 and ₹50 Cr at 94% gross margin by FY2032, converting the IP investment into a hardware-independent revenue stream. The six-chiplet combo die, if built as separate chips, would cost approximately $18M in tapeouts; as one die the engineering estimate is approximately $5M, a cost structure that keeps the end system at ₹2L rather than ₹8L, 3–7× below every comparable import.

lead: At volume, the SoC2 die costs $3.88 per unit, $2.38 wafer cost plus $1.50 assembly, test and packaging, against an incumbent ADAS SoC cost of $3,000–$8,000, a cost advantage of approximately 774×. explanation: The Per-Die Cost Stack: The SoC2 die is 57 mm² on TSMC 28 nm HPC+, processed on a 300 mm wafer priced at $2,400 at volume-committed rates. With 1,010 good die per wafer, the wafer cost per good die is $2.38; adding $1.50 for OSAT assembly, test and packaging at volume brings the total per-die cost to $3.88. The investor briefing summarises this as a ~$3 die inside a ~$30 complete board BOM, and the Information Memorandum states the die cost is <$4 at 1 million chips, figures consistent with the financial model's $3.88 calculation.

The NRE Recovery and Margin Profile: Total one-time NRE for the phased tapeout program is $3,170,000 (₹29.798 Cr), covering MPW block runs, a full 57 mm² prototype, backend GDSII, a dedicated production mask set and IP licences. At a chip contribution of $22 per chip inside a kit and a gross margin per chip of $18.12, the financial model states NRE breakeven at 174,908 chips, all management projections. At the OEM B2B product level, the bare die sold at ₹18,000 per unit with a 30,000-unit FY2032 volume target carries a 94% gross margin, the highest in the portfolio, because it arrives with no installation capacity or warranty logistics.

title: Competition
lead: DeepGrid competes against well-capitalised Western incumbents (Aurora/Kodiak-class platforms) and domestic Indian startups split between software-first players and microcontroller/SoC designers. It wins primarily on price, a single custom combo-die on TSMC 28 nm collapses the compute board BOM far below the $6,000+ Western benchmark, and on being the only Indian startup combining silicon, AI models, and ADAS software in one vertically integrated stack purpose-built for commercial-vehicle mandates.
explanation: The Competitive Field: DeepGrid faces two distinct threat clusters. Global players such as Aurora and Kodiak rely on general-purpose multi-chip GPU/CPU boards whose BOM exceeds $6,000, forcing them to target premium logistics markets in developed economies rather than India's price-sensitive fleet operators. Domestically, software-first startups (Minus Zero, Swaayatt, RoshAI) are structurally squeezed by expensive imported merchant silicon that keeps end-customer prices high, while microcontroller/SoC designers (Mindgrove, Netrasemi) build efficient chips on TSMC 12 nm/28 nm but lack the 39.3 TOPS deep-learning acceleration and specialised 77 GHz radar processing required for real-time safety compliance.

The Structural Moat: DeepGrid's primary advantage is vertical integration across all three industry layers, silicon, AI models, and ADAS software, at a time when pure-play ADAS software is entering a squeeze zone as OEMs absorb the stack from above and chipmakers push up from below. By consolidating six functional chiplets (A100, R100, T100, D100, S100, H100) onto a single ~57.1 mm² die fabricated on a mature 28 nm node, DeepGrid eliminates the multi-chip board complexity that drives Western incumbents' costs, dropping its custom die cost and complete board-level BOM to a fraction of the $6,000+ Western figure. Management describes this as the only Indian startup designing a vertically integrated, single-die ADAS combo-die tailored specifically for commercial-vehicle mandates at a disruptive price point.

Where the Differentiation Is Still Being Earned: The investment memorandum cautions that 'India-native' tuning is no longer a differentiator because four rivals already claim it; the unclaimed ground is a measured nuisance (false-positive) rate, which AIS-162 tests for explicitly. DeepGrid's stated approach is to publish a scenario-stratified false-positive rate per 1,000 km against a named baseline, covering India-specific scenarios such as overtaking two-wheelers, cattle, and unlit stationary trucks, a metric no competitor has yet published. Until an ISO 26262 assessor is engaged, however, a Tier-1 integrator is comparing a certified incumbent with an uncertified newcomer, and no perception result alone closes that gap.
facts: Western BOM Benchmark: Western incumbents' compute board BOM exceeds $6,000, versus DeepGrid's single-die design targeting a fraction of that cost at TSMC 28 nm, the primary pricing moat.

Domestic Gap: Domestic software-first rivals lack purpose-built silicon; domestic SoC rivals lack 39.3 TOPS deep-learning acceleration and specialised 77 GHz radar processing required for real-time safety.

Integration Claim: DeepGrid is, per management, the only Indian startup designing a vertically integrated single-die ADAS combo-die tailored for commercial-vehicle mandates at a disruptive price point.

Unclaimed Differentiator: No competitor has published a measured nuisance (false-positive) rate per 1,000 km stratified by India-specific scenarios, the metric AIS-162 tests for and DeepGrid's stated competitive wedge.

keywords: what are the investment risks
title: The investment risks
lead: DeepGrid Semi's own materials surface ten material risks, of which at least five are structural or unfunded rather than speculative. The most time-sensitive are a hard March 2027 IP expiry with no budget line, a regulatory timeline that the company's own claim controls prohibit citing, and a tapeout schedule that pushes qualified silicon to H1 2028, after the mandate window the revenue model is built on.
explanation: The Funding Gaps: Two dated cash calls appear in no allocation line in the use of funds. Fifteen provisional patents (IN2026/DGR/001–015, filed March 2026) must convert to complete specifications within twelve months, landing inside the round's first year, yet no conversion cost is budgeted. Separately, the ISO 26262 functional-safety assessor required to compete with certified incumbents for Tier-1 design-ins is listed as a 30-day procurement action but absent from the use-of-funds entirely, only AIS-162/188 type approval is funded. Both are hard, dated obligations whose absence from the budget means the round as structured does not close them.

The Schedule and Regulatory Risks: The FPGA-to-ASIC transition is the plan's central value inflection, but qualified volume silicon does not land until H1 2028, after the all-models mandate date, and OEM design-in cycles run 18–30 months beyond that. Every rupee before H1 2028 must therefore come through the FPGA module via government and PSU channels, a lane the fifteen-line financial model does not name as a separate revenue line, making the first eighteen months untraceable against the forecast. Compounding this, the memorandum and financial model anchor demand to GSR 184(E) from April 2026, a claim the company's own internal ledger bars as prohibited; the standards-level dates are 2027–2028, shifting first mandated revenue by roughly eighteen months.

Where the Numbers Diverge: Three document-level conflicts require resolution before the data room opens. The tapeout NRE is quoted at both $2.42M (die card) and $3.17M (platform slide and use-of-funds), a $750K difference on the single largest line item. Total FY2032 revenue appears as both ₹1,128 Cr (the memorandum's revenue slide header) and ₹1,388 Cr (the same document's tables), a ₹259.5 Cr gap across eleven product lines the business plan carries but the financial model does not size. The addressable truck pool is stated as 5M+ in the memorandum against 1.0M in the model, a difference that directly sets the capture-rate denominator for the plan's largest SKU.
facts: IP Expiry: Fifteen provisional patents expire March 2027, a hard cash call inside the round's first year with no budget line in the use of funds.

Revenue Concentration: The AD2 truck kit (₹450 Cr, 40%) and AD0 smart mirror (₹270 Cr, 24%) together represent 64% of the FY2032 plan, ₹720 Cr exposed to a single certification delay or fitment bottleneck.
Tapeout NRE Discrepancy: NRE is quoted at $2.42M in the die card and $3.17M in the platform slide and use-of-funds, a $750K gap on the plan's largest single expenditure line.

Key-Person Exposure: The founder holds 95.6% of shares and is sole commercial accountable across all four business units; the CTO, architect of the matrix ALU and radar RTL, is not yet full-time, with full-time start shown as Q1 FY28.

lead: At least six figures conflict across the materials, with the most consequential being a ₹259.5 Cr revenue-total discrepancy and a $750K gap in the single largest capital line item. explanation: Tapeout NRE and the Funding Ask: The single largest capital line item, tapeout NRE, is quoted at both $2.42M and $3.17M across the same document set, a $750K difference the Reconciliation tab confirms. The die card states $2.42M, the platform slide states $3.17M, and the model's use-of-funds uses $3.17M phased across four gates. The funding ask itself carries a parallel conflict: ₹25 Cr and ₹45 Cr appear in the same document set according to the reconciliation research, and the prior BP-1A converted ₹45 Cr to '$5.4M' against an implied USD/INR of 83.3, while the current model uses 94, producing $4.79M for the same rupee amount.

keywords: what happens if the tapeout or mandate slips
title: If the chip slips
lead: A tapeout slip pushes qualified silicon past H1 2028 into a window where the mandate has already closed, while the fixed-cost block, payroll, R&D, the remaining mask commitment, continues running at full rate with no revenue to absorb it. A mandate slip compounds the problem: at a 70% revenue miss the model still projects roughly ₹339 Cr and claims self-funding, but that scenario is a demand test, not a schedule test, and the schedule case is not modelled anywhere in the published scenarios.
explanation: The Unmodelled Risk: The three published scenarios, Bull, Bear and Downside, scale revenue at 1.2×, 0.75× and 0.3× and adjust opex as a percentage of it, making every one of them a demand test. The variable that actually breaks the plan is schedule: a six-month silicon slip moves qualified silicon past H1 2028 into a window where the mandate has already closed and the FPGA lane is competing on price. Fixed costs, payroll, R&D, the remaining mask commitment, hold at full rate because none of them are a function of revenue, and that case is not modelled anywhere. Two additional scenarios are required before a term sheet: a six-month silicon slip, and a fixed-cost floor in which opex holds at plan while revenue misses.

What the Schedule Depends On: The tapeout is currently treated as a fixed input to the plan; it is, in fact, the largest open variable in it, and five independent advisors could not make the arithmetic of Act 5, protected PSU revenue funds the tapeout, work. The tapeout is targeted within ten months of March 2026 (roughly January 2027), but that date is contingent on the raise closing, making it earlier than the deck's Q1–mid 2027 figure and conditional rather than firm. The plan as financially modelled is a fast case in which certification, tapeout and first OEM engagement all land inside 12–18 months; comparable mandate-driven hardware markets have historically taken 3–5 years from mandate announcement to stable incumbent share, making the fast case upside rather than the base. Until the tapeout decision is closed, the capacity split, the funding sequence, the Tier-1 motion and the framing of the ASIC are all downstream of an unanswered question.

Where the Numbers Diverge: The downside case in the investment memorandum shows roughly ₹339 Cr and self-funding at a 70% revenue miss, which is the argument for underwriting the silicon rather than the forecast, but this figure is a demand-miss scenario, not a schedule-slip scenario, and the two are not equivalent. The minimum cash balance in the base case is ₹10.10 Cr with the trough in FY2029, and no contingency line exists in the use of funds; a downside cash trough has not been published and is a diligence request, not a number anyone has seen. Management projects (base case only) first EBITDA-positive in FY2028 and 87.4% gross margin in FY2032, but ₹1,128 Cr of that FY2032 revenue rests on one tapeout, and a certification delay alone hits ₹720 Cr at once across the two products that carry 64% of revenue.
facts: Silicon Window: Qualified silicon lands H1 2028, after every mandate date, making the next two years an FPGA business, not an ASIC business.
Tapeout Cost: ₹25 Cr raise explicitly for tapeout and marketing (~$3 million), corroborating the planning-grade ₹20–35 Cr range; timing contingent on the raise closing.
Fixed-Cost Exposure: Payroll, R&D and the remaining mask commitment run at full rate on a slip because none are a function of revenue, this scenario is not modelled in any published case.

Kill-Criteria Gap: The playbook contains four hard disqualifiers for customer deals and zero for the company's own ₹25 Cr tapeout bet, no funding, anchor design-in, certification path or merchant-SoC parity test is formally adopted.

keywords: what is the recommended strategy
title: The strategic choice: run A for B
lead: The recommended strategy is to lead with government and PSU fleet deployments (Option A) while simultaneously opening a Tier-1 automotive exchange (Option B) in the same month, not sequentially. Government units serve as an instrumented sensor network that generates the measured nuisance-rate data required to win Tier-1 design-ins, making the pre-silicon window the foundation of the post-silicon business rather than a holding pattern.
explanation: The Core Logic: The investment memorandum is explicit that running Option A first and Option B second causes the evidence to arrive too late to matter for any Tier-1 evaluation. Instead, the two lanes must be opened concurrently so that instrumented government vehicles, with telemetry rights secured in the supply contract, produce a scenario-stratified false-positive rate per 1,000 km while the Tier-1 conversation is still open. This is the only available differentiator: four rivals already claim India-native perception, but no competitor has published a measured nuisance rate, and AIS-162 tests for exactly that. The government fleet is therefore not a survival lane but the evidence engine that makes the Tier-1 lane winnable.

The Supporting Lanes: Defence (Option C in the memorandum's framing, represented by the D-HUMR platform) is ring-fenced as a separate two-engineer lane with its own procurement route and exit vector, valued because its revenue is uncorrelated with the mandate cycle. Licensing (Option D) stays where the financial model already places it, with the T100 AI Licence projected at ₹50 Cr revenue and 94% gross margin from FY2029 onward as a management projection. Option E, drifting without a deliberate lane choice, is described as what the round becomes by default if no lane is chosen, which is itself the argument for choosing. Defence telemetry transfers nothing to the Tier-1 evidence base, which is why it cannot lead.

The Unvalidated Assumptions: The recommendation rests on four conditions that no reviewed document has confirmed. First, the bill of materials must clear 50% local content to qualify for Class-I status, which is the entire basis of the government lane, and no document computes this on actual imported-content values. Second, telemetry rights must survive a public-procurement contract, which has not been checked against any state transport undertaking's standard terms. Third, an ISO 26262 assessor, which gates the Tier-1 lane entirely, is listed as a procurement action in the company's own 30-day plan but is unfunded in the use-of-funds. Fourth, converting 15 provisional patents before the March 2027 deadline is a hard, dated cash call that appears in no allocation line.
facts: Concurrent Launch: Government fleet deployments (Option A) and Tier-1 exchange (Option B) open in the same month, not sequentially, so telemetry data is available while the Tier-1 evaluation is still live.

GeM Gate: A live GeM listing with documented local content at or above 50% and one Class-I tender bid submitted with telemetry rights in the draft contract is the proof-of-execution gate for the government lane.
Defence Lane: D-HUMR is ring-fenced as a separate two-engineer lane; management projects ₹30 Cr revenue at 68% gross margin by FY2032 at 150 units, with first revenue FY2027.
Patent Deadline: 15 provisional patents carry a March 2027 conversion deadline that is a hard, dated cash call appearing in no use-of-funds allocation line.

keywords: what is the plan for the united states
title: The US opportunity
lead: DeepGrid Semi's US plan is a licensing and stack business, not a box business, structured as a Delaware entity majority-owned by the Indian parent, with an incoming co-founder holding earned equity tranches against named commercial gates. The plan carries no US revenue forecast; it begins with three introductions the co-founder must open, and scales to a $25M follow-on round targeted for 2028, gated on India's deployment milestones being met first.
explanation: The Entry Logic: The US opportunity is framed as a licensing and soft-IP business rather than a hardware distribution play, because the regulatory environment and qualification requirements make a packaged-chip sale the last step, not the first. FMVSS 111 rules prevent the smart mirror from being sold as a mirror replacement, making it a supplementary sensor pod with a different product posture, and heavy-vehicle AEB rulemaking targets OEM factory-fit rather than retrofit. The honest sequencing management proposes is: soft-IP licence and perception model first (S2 and S6), then S1 and S3, with the packaged chip (S4) last, meaning first American revenue is management's projection to be a licence, not a part.

The Structure: A Delaware entity is proposed at inception, majority-owned by Deepgrid Semi India, which also retains all IP and grants the US entity an exclusive, territory- and field-of-use-limited licence. The co-founder holds a meaningful minority as real founder equity, not phantom shares, earned in tranches against named commercial gates, with standard leaver and reverse-vesting provisions. Four guardrails are stated: Indian parent retains majority and control; IP stays in India and does not transfer; equity is earned not granted; and ODI filing and FEMA residency must be established before any paperwork is signed.

The Sequencing and the Ask: The US plan is explicitly gated on India executing first, if the India tapeout and AIS certification slip, the 2028 US fundraise slips with it, and management states the right response is to say so rather than raise anyway. No US capital is drawn from the ₹45 Cr India round. What management is asking the co-founder for is not capital but three things: one platform or Tier-1 technical conversation (Samsara, Motive, or Netradyne class), one American yard operator willing to run a private-land pilot, and the co-founder's judgement used critically against the plan. The $25M follow-on round to compete properly is targeted at 2028, gated on a Series A, and is described as agreed in shape between both parties.
facts: Investment Terms: $1M at ₹112 Cr pre-money in two tranches with a side letter, for approximately 7.7% of the Indian company, separate from any US equity.
US Entity Structure: Delaware company, Indian parent holds majority and the exclusive US licence; IP itself stays in India, the one guardrail management states it will not move on.
US Follow-On Target: $25M follow-on round targeted for 2028, gated on Series A and on India fleet deployment delivering field-failure data and manufacturing maturity, a management projection.
Retrofit Market Size: 3.91M Class 8 trucks in operation in the US as of 2026, against a $906B trucking industry revenue base, the sourced addressable context for the licensing entry.

keywords: what is the defence and robotics opportunity
title: Defence and robotics
lead: DeepGrid's defence and robotics segment covers five SKUs with a combined FY2032 management projection of ₹83.5 Cr, equal to 7.4% of the total plan. The two defence-facing products are the D-HUMR unmanned ground vehicle at ₹20 L per unit (₹30 Cr FY2032 projection, 68% gross margin, first revenue FY2027) and the D100 Drone SoC Kit at ₹5 L per unit (₹20 Cr FY2032 projection, 68% gross margin, first revenue FY2028), with ₹1 Cr of institutional defence revenue already received on FPGA hardware.
explanation: The Strategic Logic: The D-HUMR opens a sovereign procurement channel, Indian Army and MoD programmes via GeM listing and routes such as iDEX, DRDO and MCEME, that is structurally independent of the automotive mandate driving the rest of the portfolio. Indigenous-procurement rules in defence exclude import-dependent competitors by specification rather than by price, creating near-zero competition for a compliant domestic supplier. The D100 Drone SoC Kit extends the same SoC2 die into aerial perception for airframe builders, adding a second procurement cycle for little incremental engineering because, as management states, the perception problem is the same one with the ground removed. Together these two lines give the company a sovereign customer and a procurement route that does not depend on the automotive mandate at all.

How the Products Work: Both products run on the same SoC2 compute core, which carries AES-256 encryption, dual-core lockstep RISC-V and ECC SRAM, the D100 secure enclave. On the D-HUMR, the fusion stack is pointed outward: radar, thermal and camera tracks along a perimeter are classified individually and then correlated, so a vehicle loitering on an access road and a person approaching a fence are resolved into a single threat rather than two unrelated contacts. The autonomy stack supports GPS-denied navigation, teleoperation override and a mission payload interface, with a live perimeter console already demonstrated that escalates contacts along a timed ladder from loiter to approach to breach risk while suppressing false alarms. The D100 Drone Kit applies the same silicon in a flight-weight form factor with a gimbal camera, IMU and flight-controller interface, targeting airframe builders who need airborne object detection and telemetry relay.

Revenue and Risk Profile: Management projects D-HUMR at ₹30 Cr by FY2032 at 150 units and the D100 Drone SoC Kit at ₹20 Cr at 400 units; both figures are management projections. The Investment Memorandum flags a material dependency: the ₹1 Cr of delivered defence revenue sits in a different legal entity and the IP is MCEME-owned, which it identifies as an unresolved IP position. The procurement cycle is described across multiple documents as slow and lumpy rather than technical, qualification is long, but once a platform is in, displacement is difficult, and the MCEME pipeline of ₹88 L is noted as active, providing near-term revenue visibility ahead of ASIC silicon.
facts: Segment Total: ₹83.5 Cr FY2032 management projection across 5 SKUs, equal to 7.4% of the total portfolio plan.
D-HUMR Unit Economics: ₹20 L unit price, 150 units at FY2032, ₹30 Cr revenue projection, 68% gross margin, management projection, first revenue FY2027.
D100 Drone SoC Kit Unit Economics: ₹5 L unit price, 400 units at FY2032, ₹20 Cr revenue projection, 68% gross margin, management projection, first revenue FY2028.
Existing Revenue: ₹1 Cr institutional defence revenue received on FPGA hardware Q1 2026, with MCEME pipeline of ₹88 L active; IP noted as MCEME-owned.
